questions.q: Which file does npm run dev start, and which one does npm start run?
questions.explain: The dev script is tsx watch src/server.ts and start is node dist/server.js. src/index.ts only exports createApp for tests and tools.

questions.q: Why does src/server.ts call await runtime.start() before server.start()?
questions.explain: Opening the port last means no request arrives while dependencies are still connecting. The same rule as module dependencies, one level up.
options: Because the router cannot be created before the runtime
So the integrations (a database, Redis) are connected before the first request can reach a handler that uses them
It makes no difference; the order is arbitrary

questions.q: The environment has PORT=80a. What happens when you run npm run dev?
questions.explain: Settings are loaded and checked before anything else. A bad value stops the program with a message that names the variable, before any connection is opened.
options: The server starts on the default port 3000
loadConfig throws a ConfigurationError on the first line, and nothing is started
The runtime starts, then the HTTP server fails to listen

questions.q: You wrote PostgresExamplesRepository, which implements ExamplesRepository. Which file do you change so the whole app uses it?
questions.explain: The composition root decides which implementation each layer receives. The service depends only on the interface, so nothing else changes.

questions.q: src/app.ts calls createContainer() from @zudojs/container and passes it to the runtime. What is registered in it in a freshly generated project?
questions.explain: The name is easy to confuse. The generated composition root is plain TypeScript in src/container.ts; the @zudojs/container container stays empty until you register something in it.
options: Nothing; the request objects are built by plain constructors in src/container.ts

questions.q: Which layer is the only one that knows about HTTP (status codes, request bodies, path parameters)?
questions.explain: The controller turns a request into typed input and a result into a response. The service and repository work with plain data, so they can be reused from jobs or scripts.

questions.q: Why does ExamplesService.get throw NotFoundError instead of returning a 404 response?
questions.explain: An error from @zudojs/errors carries a status code and expose: true. At the HTTP edge, errorResponse turns it into a response; elsewhere it is just an error.
options: The service stays free of HTTP, so a job or a CLI tool can call it; the error carries its status for whoever turns it into a response
Services are not allowed to import @zudojs/http by TypeScript
So the repository can catch it

questions.q: POST /api/v1/examples with {"name": ""} gets a 400. Which layers ran?
questions.explain: Input is checked at the edge. Invalid data never reaches the service, which is why the trace showed no service.create line for that request.
options: Controller, service and repository; the repository refused it
Controller and service; the service refused it
Only the controller: CreateExampleSchema.safeParse failed and it answered with validationFailed

questions.q: A client sends {name: as the body. What turns it into a 400?
questions.explain: JSON.parse fails inside readJsonBody, which throws badRequest("The request body is not valid JSON."). The catch in dispatch passes it to errorResponse.
options: The schema, which cannot parse the text
readJsonBody throws badRequest(…), an exposed 4xx error, and dispatch turns it into a response

questions.q: A repository throws new Error("disk full"). What does the client get, and what does the server log in the generated project?
questions.explain: errorResponse ignores errors without an exposed 4xx status, dispatch rethrows, and the HTTP server answers a generic 500. Nothing logs the original error, so add logging in dispatch.
options: 500 with "disk full" in the body; the error is logged
500 with {"error":"Internal Server Error"}; nothing is logged

questions.q: When does errorResponse(error) return a response instead of undefined?
questions.explain: Only client errors that are marked safe to show become responses. A 5xx or an unmarked error stays hidden behind a generic 500, so internal details never leak.
options: For every error whose statusCode is between 400 and 599
When the error has a statusCode from 400 to 499, expose: true and a string message

questions.q: Why are the controller's handlers written as public readonly list = async () => … instead of normal methods?
questions.explain: Passing controller.list as a callback detaches a normal method from its object, and this.service would be undefined. Arrow properties capture this when the object is created.
options: The router calls controller.list on its own, and an arrow function keeps this bound to the controller
TypeScript does not allow async methods in classes

questions.q: export type AppConfig = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadConfig>>; What is the benefit?
questions.explain: One source of truth. ReturnType gives the function's return type, and Awaited unwraps the Promise because loadConfig is async. AppDependencies uses the same trick.
options: It validates the config at runtime
The type follows the function: add a setting to the returned object and every file using AppConfig sees it, with no second definition to keep in sync

questions.q: A test calls loadConfig({ PORT: "4000" }). Is the developer's .env file read?
questions.explain: The check if (env === process.env) loadDotEnv() keeps tests independent of whatever is on the developer's disk.
options: No: .env is only loaded when the argument is the real process.env

questions.q: An integration has no health method. How does it appear in /health?
questions.explain: checkIntegrations skips integrations without health. Give an integration a health method when a failure of it should take the app out of rotation.
options: It is not listed, so it never makes the app unready

questions.q: While the app is shutting down, every integration still reports "up". What does /health answer?
questions.explain: Readiness includes the runtime state. Answering 503 during shutdown tells the load balancer to stop sending new requests before connections close.
options: No answer: the server is closed

questions.q: The generated tests/examples.test.ts passes. Why can the route still be unreachable in the running app?
questions.explain: A unit test of the resource cannot see the wiring. A smoke test that builds the router the way server.ts does catches it.
options: Vitest runs a different Node.js version
The test builds its own router with registerExamplesRoutes; it never goes through registerRoutes and createDependencies, where a lost registration would show
The test uses a fake repository
The test does not send JSON

questions.q: Why does src/app.ts pass handleSignals: false to createRuntime?
questions.explain: The HTTP server is not a runtime module, so only server.ts can order "stop taking requests" before "close what requests use". One owner for signals.
options: Signals do not work with tsx
server.ts handles SIGINT and SIGTERM itself, so it can stop the HTTP server before the runtime; two handlers would race
So that <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>C</kbd> kills the process immediately
The runtime cannot handle signals in development

questions.q: On SIGTERM, the generated server runs drainIntegrations, then server.stop(), then runtime.stop(). Why is runtime.stop() last?
questions.explain: Shutdown reverses startup: stop accepting work, finish it, then release what it used.
options: It closes the integrations that requests in progress may still be using, so it must wait until the server has finished them
The runtime must log the shutdown after the server

questions.q: What does the generated signal handler do when a second SIGINT arrives during shutdown?
questions.explain: The stopping flag guards the handler. Note the difference from @zudojs/runtime's own handler, which exits at once on a second signal.
options: Prints "already shutting down" and does nothing else

questions.q: A handler sets its own content-security-policy. What does the generated securityHeaders() middleware do with it?
questions.explain: It compares header names case-insensitively and only fills the gaps. That is how /docs can load its assets with a looser policy.
options: Replaces it with the default policy
Keeps the handler's header and adds only the default headers the response does not already have

questions.q: A test calls createApp({ config: await loadConfig({ NODE_ENV: "test" }) }) with no NODE_ENV in the real environment. Which environment does the runtime log?
questions.explain: The generated app reads NODE_ENV in two places. They usually agree, but not when a test passes its own environment object.
options: It throws because the two disagree

questions.q: You run three copies of the app behind a load balancer with RATE_LIMIT_MAX=300. How many requests per window can one client really make?
questions.explain: The generated rate limiter keeps its counters in the process. A shared store is needed for a limit across instances.
options: Up to 900, because each process counts in its own memory

questions.q: Which is not a consequence of the generated in-memory repositories?
questions.explain: A Map in memory is fast. Its problems are durability, sharing between instances, and the size cap that protects memory.
options: Data is lost on every restart, including each save in npm run dev
Two copies of the app see different data
Requests are slower than with a database
The store refuses new records after 10,000

questions.q: You delete the six files of the example resource. What else must change before npm run typecheck passes?
questions.explain: The wiring still refers to the deleted classes. Remove those lines, keep the markers, and the type checker confirms nothing else uses them.
options: The lines between the markers in src/container.ts (imports and examplesController) and in src/routes/index.ts (import and call)

questions.q: This is the rule from errorResponse. What does it print?
questions.explain: Only an exposed client error becomes its own response. A 503, an unexposed 409, a plain Error and a thrown string all end up as a generic 500.

questions.q: This is the generated int setting parser, simplified. What does it print?
questions.explain: Unset and blank values use the fallback. Number("1e3") is 1000, a safe integer, so it is accepted; negatives and fractions are refused.

questions.q: Middleware runs like an onion. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each middleware runs its "in" part, calls next(), and finishes after everything inside it has finished. That is why securityHeaders(), first in the list, sees the final response of every request.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An integration without health is skipped. A health check that throws counts as down instead of breaking the endpoint. And the runtime must be running for 200.

questions.q: This is the rule in securityHeaders(). What does it print?
questions.explain: Header names are compared in lowercase, so the handler's policy counts as present and is kept. Only X-Frame-Options is added.

questions.q: In a module (strict mode), what does this print?
questions.explain: Assigning to a property of a frozen object throws a TypeError in strict mode (and ES modules are always strict). The value stays 3000.

questions.q: validationFailed turns each issue's path into a string. What does this print?
questions.explain: Numbers become strings and parts are joined with dots. A problem with the whole body has an empty path, which is what a missing body produced in the lesson's error trace.

questions.q: This is the generated list setting parser. What does it print?
questions.explain: Splitting "" gives [""], so the empty-entry filter matters: without it, an empty CORS_ORIGINS would allow the origin "".
questions.code:
const list = (raw) => (raw ?? "").split(",").map((e) => e.trim()).filter((e) => e.length > 0);
console.log(JSON.stringify([list("https://a.example, https://b.example"), list(""), list(undefined), list(" ,https://c.example,, ")]));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The composition root chooses the implementation; the default is used when the caller does not pass one. Tests pass fakes the same way.

questions.q: Write toResponse(error): return { status, body: { error: message } } for an exposed client error (numeric statusCode 400-499, expose === true, string message), adding code to the body when it is a string. Return { status: 500, body: { error: "Internal Server Error" } } for anything else.
questions.explain: The second error shows why the rule exists: its message contains a secret. Only errors that were deliberately marked as safe reach the client.

questions.q: Write readPort(raw): return 3000 when raw is undefined or blank, the number when it is an integer from 0 to 65535, and otherwise throw an Error with the message PORT must be an integer between 0 and 65535, got "RAW".
questions.explain: Number("80a") is NaN, which is not an integer. Quoting the raw value in the message shows invisible mistakes such as a trailing space.
questions.expected:
3000
3000
4000
PORT must be an integer between 0 and 65535, got "80a".
PORT must be an integer between 0 and 65535, got "70000".

questions.q: Write createDependencies(options = {}) for a shop: it returns { health, ordersController }. health is options.health or a function returning { ready: true }. ordersController is new OrdersController(new OrdersService(options.repository ?? new MemoryOrders())).
questions.explain: Defaults for production, parameters for tests: the same composition root serves both, and no other layer knows which repository it got.

questions.q: Write compose(middlewares, handler) returning a function (request) => response. Each middleware is (request, next) => response, where next() runs the rest. Use it so the output below appears.
questions.explain: The header middleware is first, so it wraps everything and even the 403 gets the header, exactly like securityHeaders() first in the generated pipeline.

questions.q: The app's routes are a Map from "METHOD path" to a handler. Write smoke(routes, expected) that returns the entries of expected that have no handler, and print ok when none are missing.
questions.explain: A smoke test checks the assembled app against a list you keep by hand. Add each new resource's path to the list, and a lost registration fails the test instead of a customer's request.

questions.q: Write createShutdown(steps). It returns onSignal(name). The first call prints Received NAME: shutting down. and runs every step in order (each is a function that prints). Later calls print Received NAME again: already shutting down. and do nothing else.
questions.explain: The flag lives in a closure, so only the handler can change it. Without it, an impatient second Ctrl + C would stop the server twice.
questions.expected:
Received SIGTERM: shutting down.
drain integrations
stop http server
stop runtime
Received SIGINT again: already shutting down.

questions.q: Write the controller half of POST /orders: createOrder(body, service) returns { status: 400, issues } when body.item is not a non-empty string or body.qty is not an integer of at least 1 (list the failing field names), otherwise { status: 201, data: service.create(body) }. The service must not be called for bad input.
questions.explain: Validate at the edge, report every failing field at once, and only hand clean data inward. In the real project, a @zudojs/schema object does the checking in one safeParse.
